stories.headline: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO 11 days after he resigned
stories.dek: President Donald Trump said he "convinced" the board to reverse course; Nvidia shares jumped about 32% in New York, and lawmakers from both parties demanded answers.
stories.summary: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned over reported affairs, including with an alleged Chinese spy. Trump said he persuaded the board; Nvidia shares jumped and Wall Street rallied.
body: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive on Monday, less than two weeks after he resigned over reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman US authorities suspect of spying for China.

President Donald Trump said he had pushed for the move. "I made the deal," he told CNBC, saying he had "convinced" the board. He added: "I've been speaking to the [Nvidia] board directly and indirectly." Asked whether Huang would have returned without him, Trump said: "The answer is no. I believe my intervention was very important." The New York Times reported that Vice-President JD Vance played a key role in talks between the White House, Huang and Nvidia. Bloomberg reported the decision was made without consulting interim CEO Colette Kress.

Nvidia said in a statement that its directors had spoken to Huang and were "satisfied with respect to Mr Huang's candor and ability to lead Nvidia". It said it had received input from "senior levels" of the US government and was confident his return "poses no national security risk". It said an independent investigation into allegations that Huang was targeted by a Chinese intelligence operation would "proceed to conclusion". Chair Harvey Jones said the board believed reinstatement was in the interests of stockholders, employees, partners and customers.
Trump said the government had no "evidence that [Jensen Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct" and that Attorney General Todd Blanche felt Huang was "exonerated".

Nvidia shares rose 32% on Monday according to The Guardian, adding more than $1tn to its market value. The Nasdaq composite rose 6.5%, the S&P 500 rose 4.7%, and the US dollar reached a 19-month high. Nvidia's shares had fallen by a quarter after Huang resigned on November 12, alongside a wider sell-off in AI-linked stocks.

Reaction in Congress was critical across party lines. Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision "reckless" and said Huang still owed Congress answers on compliance with chip export restrictions. Senator Ruben Gallego, a Democrat, called for an investigation into stock positions taken before the announcement. Republican Senator John Cornyn asked on X: "No national security risk? Based on what". Senator Rick Scott said the move "looks terrible on its face", and Senator Katie Britt said Huang "must answer" for his actions. Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "does not support reinstatement".

Senate Banking Committee Chair Tim Scott announced Huang would appear before the panel on December 3, according to Fox News. The Guardian reported the date for his congressional testimony as December 1. TechCrunch reported he is also expected to testify privately before several House committees next month.
The White House did not respond to Fox News' request for comment.
keyFacts: Huang resigned on November 12 and was reinstated on Monday, November 23.
Nvidia shares rose 32% on Monday, adding more than $1tn in value, per The Guardian.
The Nasdaq composite rose 6.5% and the S&P 500 rose 4.7%.
Huang is due to testify to the Senate in early December; sources give December 1 and December 3.
Trump told CNBC he "convinced" the board; Nvidia cited input from senior US officials.
stories.background: Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. He resigned after reports of affairs, including with Alice Huang (no relation), formerly of Singapore-based Megaspeed, and two Nvidia employees. US authorities are investigating Megaspeed over suspected diversion of chips to China in breach of export controls. Megaspeed calls itself a "legitimate and lawful business" and says Alice Huang no longer works there. Beijing denies the spying allegation.
stories.whyItMatters: Nvidia's chips underpin much of the AI industry, and its leadership drove a sharp swing in global share prices. Congressional hearings will test questions on chip exports to China.

perspectives.label: Trump and Nvidia's board
perspectives.summary: Trump said the government had no evidence of unlawful conduct by Huang and that the country needs his leadership. Nvidia said its board was satisfied with Huang and that his return poses no national security risk.

perspectives.label: Democratic lawmakers
perspectives.summary: Democrats called the move reckless and demanded a congressional investigation, citing national security, export controls and possible trading ahead of the announcement. Gallego said Trump's role was "as close to socialism, communism as I've ever seen".

perspectives.label: Republican lawmakers
perspectives.summary: Several Republicans questioned the national security basis for the decision and called for Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to answer questions in the Senate. Britt said it was Nvidia's right to reinstate him.

stories.headline: Zelenskyy says Ukrainian drones sank Russian corvette at Libya's Benghazi base
stories.dek: Eastern Libya's government has asked the UN to investigate suspicions that the drones were launched from the west, where Ukrainian personnel are alleged to operate.
stories.summary: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury and hit a cargo ship off Benghazi on Sunday. Libya's eastern government has asked the UN to investigate claims of a Ukrainian military presence in the west.
body: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukrainian naval drones sank the Russian corvette Merkury and hit the cargo vessel MV Angara off the Libyan city of Benghazi on Sunday, an attack some 2,400 km from the front line in Ukraine.

Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian-made drones were used and that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was destroyed with the corvette. In a post on X he called it "an exemplary Ukrainian operation" and said "the targets we set were achieved." He said the Angara was used to carry weapons. Ukraine's Security Service said the ship was sanctioned and the Merkury had escorted Russian convoys, including the Angara.

Accounts of the damage differ. Two Libyan officials told the Associated Press the corvette was severely damaged, not sunk. They said at least four drones were intercepted and two hit the ship, and that at least 10 people, Libyan and Russian nationals, were wounded. The officials are affiliated with the Libyan National Army and spoke anonymously.

Local authorities said an explosion hit the warship early on Sunday as it docked at the Benghazi naval base for fuel and supplies. The eastern government said the Russian ship was using the port under an existing maritime agreement. It did not name the vessel. Ambrey, a maritime security firm, said some explosions were likely caused by ammunition aboard the Merkury. Videos geolocated by BBC Verify and Planet Labs satellite imagery showed a burning vessel at the port.

Hours later, the Libyan coast guard said, another sea drone hit a Maltese-flagged commercial vessel off Benghazi. The local health ministry said it received injured people from a commercial ship. It is not clear whether that is the Angara.

Osama Hamad, prime minister of the eastern-based government, said he asked the United Nations to investigate "suspicions that the boats had been launched from western Libya" and to verify whether Ukrainian military experts operate there. The east's government sent a letter to Secretary-General António Guterres and the Security Council. It has accused the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity of hosting Ukrainian personnel. The Tripoli government did not immediately respond to Fox News, but said in a statement it would not be drawn into the conflict and that foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports for military purposes.

The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" and called for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on Libya, saying Russia's Defence Ministry would provide information. He warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region" after a separate drone attack on the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday.
keyFacts: Zelenskyy said seven Ukrainian naval drones struck the corvette Merkury and cargo ship MV Angara on Sunday.
Two Libyan officials told AP the Merkury was severely damaged, not sunk; at least 10 people were wounded.
Eastern Libya's government asked the UN to investigate claims of Ukrainian forces operating in western Libya.
Benghazi is about 2,400 km from the front line in Ukraine, according to AP.
stories.background: Libya has been split since Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, between the UN-recognised government in Tripoli and a rival administration in the east. Libyan officials told AP earlier this year that Ukrainian drone experts operate in western Libya under a covert deal endorsed by the West, including at an air base in Misrata. Eastern commander Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army has longstanding links with Russia.
stories.whyItMatters: The strike draws Libya, whose rival governments say they are not parties to the war, into the Russia-Ukraine conflict and raises the question of which foreign forces operate on its territory.

perspectives.label: Ukraine
perspectives.summary: Zelenskyy described the strike as a response to Russian aggression and said the targets were achieved. Ukraine's Security Service said the Angara was sanctioned and used to move military equipment.

perspectives.label: Eastern Libya
perspectives.summary: The eastern government called the attack a violation of maritime safety and sovereignty, and said the Russian ship was in port under an agreement. It asked the UN to investigate possible launches from western Libya.

perspectives.label: Tripoli government and UN
perspectives.summary: Tripoli said it would not be drawn into the conflict and would bar foreign military use of its ports. The UN mission called for an independent investigation.

stories.headline: India announces ₹15,000 crore package for Nepal during Balendra Shah's Delhi visit
stories.dek: Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Nepal's Balendra Shah also signed eight MoUs and launched the Ayodhya–Janakpur train, a border bridge and energy projects.
stories.summary: India announced a ₹15,000 crore development package for Nepal after Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks with Nepal's Balendra Shah in New Delhi on Monday. The two leaders signed eight MoUs and launched cross-border rail, bridge, hydropower and pipeline projects.
body: India announced a ₹15,000 crore development package for Nepal on Monday after Prime Minister Narendra Modi held talks in New Delhi with his Nepalese counterpart, Balendra Shah, on Shah's first bilateral visit abroad since taking office in March.

The Ministry of External Affairs said, as reported by Scroll, that the package comprises ₹3,500 crore in grants for reconstruction and infrastructure after August's floods and a ₹11,500 crore line of credit for energy projects. Scroll put the sum at about 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees. Firstpost and the BBC gave the equivalent as roughly $1.6 billion.
The leaders jointly launched the Sarayu-Kamala Express between Ayodhya in Uttar Pradesh and Janakpur in Nepal. They inaugurated a motorable bridge between Dharchula in India and Darchula in Nepal.

They laid the foundation stone for a new Integrated Check Post at Banbasa in Uttarakhand's Champawat district and reviewed progress on check posts at Bhairahawa, Sunauli and Dodhara Chandani. In energy, they laid the foundation stone for the 669 MW Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project and dedicated Phase II of the Motihari–Amlekhgunj Pipeline. A foundation stone was also laid for a petroleum terminal at Jhapa, for the proposed Siliguri-Jhapa petroleum pipeline.

Firstpost reported that eight MoUs were signed, covering policing, forensic sciences, civil service training, traditional medicine, satellite communication, sustainable urban development, healthcare, and livestock and fisheries. One links Isro with Nepal's Ministry of Information and Communication on a satellite communication network using the South Asia Satellite.

Modi said India would help set up a start-up incubator, an innovation hub and an offshore campus of the Indian Institute of Technology in Nepal. He said India would also expand scholarships in law and technology for Nepali students and help develop an agro-industrial park for food processing.

Modi said the relationship "is not merely one of neighbours, but one of kinship and unbreakable trust". He said India had kept supplies of fuel, fertilisers and other essentials flowing to Nepal despite disruptions to global oil supplies. He also expressed condolences for those killed in the August floods.
Shah said the ties "stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as the ocean". He invited Indian investors to Nepal and called for expanded direct air connectivity between cities of both countries.

The BBC reported that Nepal also secured access to two more Indian ports, Kandla and Paradip, and that India agreed to make the Kathmandu–Bhairahawa–Lucknow air route bidirectional. It said Nepal's request for wider access to Indian airspace for its Bhairahawa and Pokhara airports was not met. The border dispute was largely absent from public remarks, though the joint statement acknowledged that outstanding issues remain, the BBC said.
keyFacts: India announced a ₹15,000 crore package: ₹3,500 crore in grants and ₹11,500 crore in credit.
Eight MoUs were signed, covering areas from policing to satellite communication.
The Sarayu-Kamala Express links Ayodhya and Janakpur.
The Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project is 669 MW.
Shah is on a two-day visit, his first bilateral trip abroad since taking office in March.
stories.background:
Shah, a former Kathmandu mayor and rapper, became prime minister after his Rastriya Swatantra Party won 182 of 275 seats in the March 5 election, the first since youth-led protests toppled the KP Sharma Oli government in September last year.

Floods and a mudslide in Nepal's Rasuwa district on August 26 left hundreds dead and thousands missing. Sources gave differing tolls: Scroll cited at least 675 dead and more than 2,420 missing, while Firstpost cited around 1,500 dead and 5,200 missing.
stories.whyItMatters: The package funds flood reconstruction and energy projects in Nepal, while new rail, bridge and border-post links affect trade and travel between Nepal and Indian states including Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks in Antalya end without a deal after dispute over fossil fuels
stories.dek: The EU and about 130 countries rejected a cover text that omitted any fossil fuel phase-out, while Saudi Arabia, Russia, India and China backed the draft.
stories.summary: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday with no consensus agreement after the EU and others rejected a draft that did not mention fossil fuels. Saudi Arabia has been accused of leading the opposition to such language.
body: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday without a consensus agreement after the European Union and other countries rejected a draft that did not mention moving away from fossil fuels, following 48 hours of overtime.

The Hindu reported that about 130 countries backed the EU position, roughly two-thirds of those represented, according to the BBC. The text at issue was the cover decision, called the Antalya Pact, proposed by COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister. The New York Times said it was the first time UN climate talks had broken down over a final agreement since COP15 in Copenhagen in 2009.

Ireland's Climate Minister Darragh O'Brien, speaking for the EU, said: "We will not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuel." Panama's chief climate negotiator, Ana Aguilar, said the text weakened language agreed in earlier decisions and relied too heavily on carbon capture technologies. "This is a setback, a rollback," she said.

Saudi Arabia, Russia and other oil producers opposed any mention of fossil fuels, according to the New York Times. Mohammad Ayoub, a Saudi negotiator speaking for the 22 Arab League countries, said Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical emissions and had the right to choose their own approach. Russia's delegate, Sergei Kononuchenko, said: "For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel."

India, China and Saudi Arabia, all part of the Like Minded Developing Countries group, said they were comfortable with the text's framing but raised concerns about adaptation finance and equity. India's Environment Minister Bhupendra Yadav said "climate ambition must go hand in hand with means of implementation." Amandeep Garg, speaking for the group, said it was willing to move forward despite its discomfort with parts of the text.

CNA reported that Saudi Arabia pushed for carbon capture and storage to be included instead. The International Monetary Fund forecasts a 3.3 per cent drop in Saudi GDP this year, and oil made up 52 per cent of public income in the first nine months of 2026, according to the finance ministry. Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman said at the summit: "What unites us is the goal, and not necessarily the path to reach it."

The BBC noted the United States sent no official delegation. Climate finance was a second dispute: Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa said Europe had refused to acknowledge its own responsibility on finance, and the BBC said the EU had ruled out significant new funding before the talks.

Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who co-led the negotiations, cited "the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory". UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on how to "improve, modernise and reform" the process. Some governments have proposed voting when consensus fails, while others want willing countries to act outside the formal talks, the BBC reported.
keyFacts: COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, ended on Sunday, November 22, 2026, after 48 hours of overtime.
About 130 countries backed the EU demand for explicit fossil fuel language.
It is the first COP breakdown over a final deal since Copenhagen in 2009.
COP28 in Dubai agreed to transition away from fossil fuels; the Antalya draft did not mention them.
UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on reforming the COP process.
stories.background: Climate summit decisions need the consensus of all 190-plus parties, so no country or bloc holds a formal veto, but any one can block a text. Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels.
stories.whyItMatters: Without a cover decision, the summit produced no overall political outcome, and the dispute over the consensus rule has prompted proposals to change how UN climate talks operate.

stories.headline: US sanctions dozens tied to Iran's shadow banking; Tehran vows to counter blockade
stories.dek: Iran's Foreign Ministry said the US blockade and sanctions amount to military aggression, and that Tehran may use any means to defend itself under Article 51 of the UN Charter.
stories.summary: The US Treasury sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front companies and officials on Monday, saying they sustain Iran's foreign trade. Iran said it would use all available means against the US naval blockade, and Al Jazeera reported renewed attacks on Gulf targets.
body: The US Treasury Department on Monday imposed sanctions on dozens of people and entities that it said run Iran's "shadow banking" networks, widening its effort to cut Iran off from the global economy.

Treasury said the targets included about two dozen Iranian exchange houses and front companies, among them firms based in the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong, along with key personnel. Fox News reported that the Office of Foreign Assets Control carried out the action and that 10 of the front companies are in those three jurisdictions.

Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network also released an analysis. It identified about $14.7 billion of financial activity from January 2025 to August 2026 that was potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking. The analysis showed a decrease in volume over the period, which FinCEN said "may be indicative of at least partial disruption of Iran's ability to operate shadow banking networks." It also found the networks remain connected, most prominently in the UAE, Hong Kong and Singapore, through oil, shipping and investment businesses.

Treasury said the system is overseen by the Central Bank of Iran and relies on Iran-based exchange houses and "rahbar companies", bank affiliates that manage sanctions-evasion networks. Named targets include the Iran Center for Exchange of Currency and Gold and Rahbar Bazargani Nesim Baharan Qeshm Company, the affiliate of Bank Sarmayeh, and three of its officials.

Under the order, US-based assets of those designated, and of businesses 50% or more owned by them, are frozen and Americans are barred from dealing with them. Treasury also warned that foreign banks risk losing access to US correspondent accounts if they knowingly facilitate significant transactions for the networks.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a statement: "Iran's economy is underwater, and its leaders are panicking." He added that Treasury would keep dismantling the networks "until we have buried the head of the snake."

Separately, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said at a weekly briefing that Iran would "use all available means to counter U.S. aggression". He described the sanctions, economic blockade and naval blockade as "an act of military aggression against Iran" and cited Article 51 of the UN Charter.

Al Jazeera reported that Iran has hit US bases and civilian sites in the Gulf after a lull, and has stepped up attacks in recent days as the blockade and sanctions hurt its economy. The summaries available did not give details of the attacks.

Baqaei said Hormuz could reopen within two days, but only if Washington accepts Iran's demands, which include lifting the blockade. Diplomatic efforts have been stalled since a June deal collapsed, The Hindu reported.
keyFacts: Treasury sanctioned more than two dozen Iranian exchange houses, front firms and officials on Monday.
FinCEN identified about $14.7 billion in potentially linked activity from January 2025 to August 2026.
Front companies targeted are based in the UAE, Turkey and Hong Kong.
Iran says it will use 'all available means' against the US naval blockade.
stories.background:
War between Iran and the United States began on February 28, when US-Israeli strikes killed Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, according to The Hindu. Iran retaliated with missile and drone strikes across the region, and groups it backs in Lebanon, Yemen and Iraq joined the fighting.

Iran has sought to block the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway vital to global energy supplies. The US responded with a blockade of Iranian ports, economic sanctions and a task force to disrupt land routes into Iran. Fox News said Bessent launched a financial pressure campaign, Operation Economic Outcast, on August 24.
stories.whyItMatters: The sanctions put banks and firms in the UAE, Turkey, Hong Kong and elsewhere at risk of losing US access if they handle Iranian transactions. Stalled talks leave the Strait of Hormuz, key to global energy supplies, at the centre of the dispute.

perspectives.label: United States
perspectives.summary: Treasury says Iran's shadow banking is the last financial lifeline of a bankrupt regime and that it will keep dismantling the networks. Bessent said Iran's leaders are panicking.

perspectives.label: Iran
perspectives.summary: Tehran says sanctions and the blockades are military aggression and that it is entitled under Article 51 of the UN Charter to defend itself by any means. It says security can return to Hormuz if Washington meets its commitments.

stories.headline: Supreme Court tells Bengal SIR tribunals to hear deleted voters' appeals first
stories.dek: The bench asked the Election Commission to add tribunals and find new premises, and told them to hear Kolkata civic-area appeals within a week.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court directed West Bengal's appellate tribunals to hear appeals by voters deleted in the special intensive revision before challenges to inclusions, which may be deferred. It also ordered more tribunals, citing 38.31 lakh appeals filed so far.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday directed the appellate tribunals hearing challenges from West Bengal's special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls to take up appeals by deleted voters first, and to defer appeals against the inclusion of other voters for the time being.

A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana told the tribunals to sort appeals into two groups. The first is appeals by voters whose names were deleted. The second is appeals by people aggrieved by others' inclusion. Of the second group, the court said: "The second set of appeals does not involve any urgency, and those appeals may, for the time being, be deferred."
According to Hindustan Times, 38.31 lakh appeals have been filed, of which 22.21 lakh seek restoration of deleted names and 16.10 lakh challenge inclusions.

The court also ordered priority for deleted voters from the Kolkata Municipal Corporation area, where municipal elections are expected before December 7. Scroll, citing The Hindu, reported that these appeals are to be heard within a week.

The bench directed the Election Commission of India (ECI), in consultation with the chief justice of the Calcutta High Court, to increase the strength of the 19 tribunals. It also asked the commission to identify alternative premises in Kolkata. Scroll reported that the court suggested central Kolkata or the area near the airport.

Advocate Prashant Bhushan, appearing for the petitioners, told the court that only a little over one lakh appeals had been decided. He said 93% of those decided had gone in favour of deleted voters. He added that more than two lakh voters in the Kolkata municipal area had been excluded and their appeals were pending.

The bench issued the directions while hearing submissions on the 16.10 lakh appeals filed by officials of the West Bengal chief electoral officer's office against inclusions. Senior advocate Gopal Sankaranarayanan questioned the legal basis for those appeals. He argued that the chief electoral officer had no authority to challenge, in the commission's name, decisions of electoral registration officers. He cited Rule 23, under which such appeals go to an officer designated by the ECI.

In an affidavit in October, the ECI said officers of the chief electoral officer's office had filed the appeals in their statutory capacity under the Representation of the People Act, 1950, and that the matters had not come before the commission. Hindustan Times reported that the affidavit did not name anyone who authorised the filing of the 16.10 lakh appeals.
keyFacts: The bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana issued the directions on Monday.
Of 38.31 lakh appeals, 22.21 lakh seek restoration of names and 16.10 lakh challenge inclusions.
Prashant Bhushan told the court only a little over one lakh appeals have been decided.
Kolkata municipal area appeals are to be heard first; municipal elections are expected before December 7.
stories.background: The SIR in West Bengal preceded the April Assembly elections. Scroll reported that final rolls published in February initially excluded more than 61 lakh voters, and that about 91 lakh had been removed by April 6. The tribunals, headed by former High Court judges, were set up after a Supreme Court order on March 10 and began hearing appeals in April. In September, the ECI told the court it was considering raising their number to 42.
stories.whyItMatters: Deleted voters, including more than two lakh in the Kolkata municipal area according to the petitioners, may get their appeals heard before the civic elections expected by December 7.

perspectives.summary: Prashant Bhushan said the pending deletion appeals warranted priority, and that 93% of the roughly one lakh appeals decided had gone in favour of deleted voters.

stories.headline: Saurav Das says he was stopped at Delhi airport from flying to London for Oxford talk
stories.dek: The Cockroach Janta Party leader says immigration staff told him his passport had been flagged; a Delhi Police official said the force is not aware of the matter.
stories.summary: Cockroach Janta Party leader Saurav Das said on Monday he was stopped at Delhi airport from boarding a 1 am flight to London for a University of Oxford talk. A Delhi Police official said the force was unaware of the matter.
body: Saurav Das, a leader of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), said on Monday that he was stopped at Delhi's Indira Gandhi International Airport from boarding a flight to London, where he was due to speak at the University of Oxford.
Das said he was told at the immigration counter that his passport had been flagged. His flight was scheduled for 1 am. Reports describe him as a spokesperson, co-convener or activist of the CJP.

"I have been stopped by this cowardly Modi Govt at the Delhi Airport from flying to London to deliver a lecture at the University of Oxford," Das wrote on X. The Indian Express reported that he did not disclose any specific reason the authorities gave him.

In a video posted on Instagram and X, Das said Oxford's students' union had invited him. He said he had also been invited by Cambridge, the London School of Economics and Edinburgh to speak on the "cockroach movement". He said the incident would not deter him and that he would travel to London, Paris and other places in future.

A Delhi Police official told Hindustan Times the force was not aware of the matter and that immigration officials were involved. News18 reported that the government had not yet responded to the allegations. None of the reports carried a statement from immigration authorities or the Union government.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke backed Das on X. He wrote that someone in power was "jealous" of Das receiving an Oxford invitation. In a separate post, quoted by The Times of India, he said he wished Das had committed financial fraud, as the government would then have allowed him to fly.
The CJP said in a post on X that the government "fears educated voices so much that it has stooped to stopping those who carry India's voice to the world".

Das, CJP co-convenor Ashutosh Ranka and leader Ajinkya Shinde, along with 11 others, were accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar on October 13. The site had been de-notified as a protest venue, and the group was protesting against alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Das and Ranka were held in Tihar jail and released on October 21 after furnishing personal and surety bonds of ₹50,000 each.

stories.headline: Madurai bans gatherings as Supreme Court allows lamp on Thiruparankundram hill
stories.dek: A Tamil Nadu government report says the structure at the centre of the dispute is a survey pillar, as the state seeks review of the court's order.
stories.summary: Madurai's collector imposed prohibitory orders from 9 pm on November 23 until 10 am on November 25, ahead of a Supreme Court-permitted one-time lamp lighting on Thiruparankundram hill. The Tamil Nadu government has sought a review, and a state report calls the structure a survey pillar.
body: Authorities in Tamil Nadu's Madurai district imposed prohibitory orders on Monday evening banning large gatherings ahead of the Karthigai Deepam festival on November 24, after the Supreme Court allowed a lamp to be lit on a disputed pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill.

District Collector and District Magistrate Nishant Krishna issued the order under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which replaced Section 144 of the CrPC. It takes effect at 9 pm on November 23 and runs until 10 am on November 25, unless withdrawn earlier.

The order cites reports from the Madurai City Police Commissioner, the District Superintendent of Police and the Revenue Divisional Officer of Thirumangalam. They flagged mobilisation by organisations both for and against lighting the lamp at the pillar, which stands close to the Sikandar Badusha Dargah. Authorities warned that people from both communities, including from other districts, could gather in large numbers.
The order bars assemblies, agitations, demonstrations, processions and public meetings across the district. It also prohibits people from climbing the hill.

Exemptions cover gatherings authorised by competent authorities, weddings, funerals and specified domestic occasions. Ceremonies by authorised personnel of the Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy Temple are exempt, as are steps to implement the Supreme Court's November 20 order. Existing religious observances at customary locations, and lawful activity and access to the Dargah and other institutions on the hill, are protected subject to police regulation.

On November 20, the Supreme Court permitted a team authorised by the temple administration to light the lamp on the pillar, which petitioners call the Deepathoon, on November 24 as a one-time measure. The court said this creates no permanent customary, religious or proprietary right over the site, and does not displace existing observances near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple.

The state government has filed a review petition seeking reconsideration and a stay. NDTV reported that it was not listed for hearing on Monday, and that consideration before the ceremony appears unlikely unless the state obtains a special hearing.
The Hindu reported, citing a Tamil Nadu government report, that the structure atop the hill is a survey pillar. Only the headline of that report was available to Meridian.

The order has divided political parties. DMK president M K Stalin has questioned the government's handling of the case, and the BJP has criticised the state for challenging the permission. The VCK, part of the ruling alliance, has voiced strong reservations, and its president Thol Thirumavalavan has cautioned that communal forces could use the development to create tensions. Left parties have raised concern about disturbing longstanding religious arrangements.

Two other allies have said they will back the government's decision. Higher Education Minister P Viswanathan told NDTV: "The Tamil Nadu government's stand on Deepam is the Congress' stand." The Indian Union Muslim League also said it would abide by the decision.

Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay has held discussions with senior legal and police officials, including Advocate General Vijay Narayan, but has made no unequivocal public statement on how the government will proceed, NDTV reported.

stories.background: The dispute concerns lighting the Karthigai Deepam on a stone pillar atop Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai, near the Sikandar Badusha Dargah. Existing customary observances take place near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple, and the broader question of customary and religious rights remains unresolved.
stories.whyItMatters: Residents of Madurai district face restrictions on assembly and on climbing the hill until the morning of November 25, while the state and its allies disagree over how to act on the court's order.

stories.headline: Russia accuses Estonia of hostile acts, as NATO and Finland respond to incidents
stories.dek: NATO is sending early-warning aircraft to Poland after a missile incident, and Finland summoned Russia's ambassador over a suspected airspace violation by a Russian helicopter.
stories.summary: Moscow accused Estonia of hostile actions that Reuters said put it on the 'verge of triggering open war'. NATO said it will send early-warning aircraft to Poland, and Finland summoned Russia's ambassador.
body: Russia accused Estonia on Monday of hostile actions that Moscow said put Tallinn on the verge of triggering open war, according to Reuters and Al Jazeera.

Al Jazeera reported that Moscow cited Estonia's border closure and claimed Tallinn was allowing Ukraine to launch attacks. The sources available did not include Estonia's response or further detail of the Russian statement.

Separately, Reuters reported that NATO will send early-warning system aircraft to Poland after an incident involving missiles. The material available gave no further detail on the incident or the deployment.

Finland said on Monday it had summoned Russia's ambassador over a suspected violation of Finnish airspace by a Russian helicopter. The suspected breach came hours after a Ukrainian drone hit the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in international waters in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday, France 24 reported.

The strike caused a fire and the crew was evacuated; one crew member suffered minor wounds. The ship drifted into Finnish waters and anchored about 90 kilometres east of Helsinki. Finnish authorities, helped by Estonian and Russian rescue vessels, put out the fire, and the vessel was towed to Russia on Sunday evening.

In a statement on X, Finland's foreign ministry condemned what it called Russia's 'illegal war of aggression' and its escalating strikes on civilian targets in Ukraine. It called Russia's 'dangerous and reckless actions in Europe' unacceptable and said it stood in solidarity with Denmark, Poland and other European partners. It also said: 'Ukraine has the right to defend itself against Russia's illegal aggression.'

Also on Monday, Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia's Security Council, wrote in the Moscow Journal of International Law that a preventive nuclear strike by Russia could be possible in certain circumstances, Fox News reported, citing excerpts from the state news agency TASS. He cited scenarios including catastrophic non-nuclear attacks or hidden transfers of nuclear weapons to Kyiv.
Medvedev wrote that no decision to use nuclear weapons in Ukraine had been taken because there was no direct necessity. He said any final decision rests with President Vladimir Putin.
keyFacts: Russia accused Estonia of hostile actions on Monday, citing its border closure, according to Al Jazeera.
NATO will send early-warning aircraft to Poland after a missile incident, Reuters reported.
Finland summoned Russia's ambassador over a suspected helicopter airspace violation.

stories.background: The Sparta II was towed from Finnish waters to Russia on Sunday evening. Medvedev's article followed a November 19 meeting in Shenzhen of Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, where Fox News said the leaders agreed to pursue talks on reducing nuclear risks.
stories.whyItMatters: The exchanges involve three states bordering Russia or its waters, Estonia, Finland and Poland, all of which are NATO members or partners of members, and add to strain over the war in Ukraine.

stories.headline: No Winter Session dates announced 103 days after Monsoon Session ended
stories.dek: Parliament has not been prorogued, and Congress leaders have criticised the silence; the government has given no explanation for the delay.
stories.summary: The Centre has announced no dates for the Winter Session of Parliament, 103 days after the Monsoon Session ended on August 13. Congress leaders have criticised the delay, while the government has offered no official explanation.
body: The Centre has not announced dates for the Winter Session of Parliament, 103 days after the Monsoon Session was adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026, according to data from the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs cited by NDTV.

The gap exceeds the 25-year average of about 95 days between the end of the Monsoon Session and the start of the Winter Session, excluding 2020, when no Winter Session was held. It is also longer than the gaps in 2025 (102 days), 2016 (96 days) and 2004 (97 days). The longest recorded gaps were 126 days in 2017 and 123 days in 2018; the shortest was 66 days in 2007.

The Monsoon Session has also not been prorogued. Congress Lok Sabha MP Manish Tewari said on November 21 that no prorogation had taken place 100 days after adjournment. He listed earlier Monsoon Sessions in which prorogation followed within 20 to 28 days, and called the situation a "flagrant breach of parliamentary conventions". He tagged Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla in his post.

Congress spokesman Jairam Ramesh said the country should know when the Winter Session will be held, or when the Monsoon Session will be reconvened as a special session. He said the Prime Minister and Home Minister were "trapped by its own bluff and bluster" and that "there is something truly sinister that is being planned." He also said the nation was entitled to know the government's formula for delimitation.

There is no official government explanation for the delay, and no formal announcement on the Winter Session schedule has been made. Ramesh and other opposition leaders have alleged the timing is linked to a delimitation or women's reservation bill. Some media reports, citing unnamed sources, say key legislation is being prepared. NDTV noted that no official evidence has been presented to confirm either claim.

The Hindu reported that speculation has grown about a short special session to consider a delimitation Bill. It said the Winter Session has been skipped only four times in India's parliamentary history, each linked to exceptional circumstances: the Emergency, premature dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the assassination of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, and the COVID-19 pandemic.
Winter Sessions were historically convened in the second half of November, but December starts have become more common. Four of the last eight began in December, against three between 2000 and 2016.
keyFacts: The Monsoon Session was adjourned sine die on August 13, 2026.
As of November 23, the gap stood at 103 days, against a 25-year average of about 95.
The longest earlier gaps before a Winter Session were 126 days in 2017 and 123 days in 2018.
The Winter Session has been skipped only four times in India's parliamentary history, according to The Hindu.
The government has given no official explanation for the delay.
stories.background:
Parliament is adjourned sine die at the end of a session and later prorogued, which formally ends it. Tewari cited earlier Monsoon Sessions in which prorogation came within 20 to 28 days of adjournment.

Opposition leaders have linked the delay to a possible delimitation or women's reservation bill. NDTV said these are allegations and speculation, not established facts.
stories.whyItMatters: The timing of the session determines when Parliament can take up legislation, including a delimitation Bill that opposition leaders and some reports say is being prepared.

stories.headline: NATO chief vows space defence after reports Russia may launch nuclear satellite
stories.dek: German media, citing Western intelligence, say a launch could come within 60 days; the Kremlin called the reports unsubstantiated and Russia's embassy in Berlin called them propaganda.
stories.summary: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said the alliance would defend against threats in space after German media reported that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite within weeks. The Kremlin dismissed the reports as unsubstantiated.
body: NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said on Monday the alliance would defend against threats in space, responding to German media reports that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite into orbit within weeks.

The reports, published on November 23 by broadcasters WDR and NDR and the newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung, said Western intelligence agencies believe Russia has assembled a satellite called "Sputnik-S". It has reportedly been stored in the Moscow region for several years. The South China Morning Post said the reports cited unnamed German military and BND intelligence sources.

According to the German investigation, intelligence warnings shared among several NATO countries in early November said the satellite, reportedly designed to carry a nuclear warhead, could be launched within 60 days. Germany's military Space Command reportedly judged a December launch possible. Senior officials, including Defence Minister Boris Pistorius, were reportedly briefed.

Speaking in Berlin alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Rutte said: "I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory," according to Reuters. He said NATO's defence planning covered space and that the alliance had response options not always visible to the public. Merz called the allegations "shocking" but said concerns about Russia's nuclear ambitions in space were not entirely new.

The Kremlin rejected the reports. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters: "We haven’t seen the report. But there are so many ‘alleged’ and ‘possible’ claims in it, attributed to who knows whom, that it’s certainly hardly worth taking them seriously." Russia's embassy in Berlin called the reporting part of a propaganda campaign and said Moscow's space activities were peaceful and in line with international obligations.

Fox News noted that it was not clear whether the satellite already carries a warhead, or whether Western intelligence has independently verified the reported launch preparations. It said it had asked the White House, the Pentagon, US Space Command and the German embassy for comment.

The reports emerged four days after US President Donald Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen. The three leaders issued a joint declaration that nuclear war should never be fought, without binding arms-control commitments, Fox News reported.
keyFacts: German outlets reported on November 23 that Russia may launch a nuclear-armed satellite within 60 days.
The satellite is reportedly called "Sputnik-S" and has been stored near Moscow for several years.

The Kremlin said the reports were hardly worth taking seriously.
The US Defense Intelligence Agency said in October that Russia is developing such a satellite.
stories.background:
The US Defense Intelligence Agency's 2026 Challenges to Security in Space assessment said Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. Fox News reported that the agency warned such a weapon could cause rapid loss or degradation of thousands of satellites. The Biden administration acknowledged in February 2024 that Russia was developing an anti-satellite capability, while saying none had been deployed.

The 1967 Outer Space Treaty prohibits stationing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in space.
stories.whyItMatters: Satellites support GPS navigation, communications, financial transactions and weather forecasting, and Ukraine's military relies on satellite links including Starlink, according to Fox News. A nuclear detonation in orbit could affect many of them at once.

stories.headline: UK sanctions Myanmar's Min Aung Hlaing and four others after ICJ genocide ruling
stories.dek: Fourteen countries, including the UK, issued a joint statement acknowledging the court's finding and calling on Myanmar to comply with it.
stories.summary: Britain on Monday sanctioned Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing and four other senior military figures, and said it formally recognises genocide against the Rohingya. It also announced £8 million in new funding.
body: Britain on Monday imposed sanctions on five senior Myanmar military figures, including President Min Aung Hlaing, and said it formally recognises genocide against the Rohingya, days after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide in 2017.

The Foreign Office said the measures include asset freezes and travel bans. The others named are Myo Htut Hlaing, Myo Min Tun, Myat Thet Oo, Kyaw Soe and Kyaw Swar Oo. Min Aung Hlaing was already sanctioned by the UK in 2021.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said Min Aung Hlaing was "directly responsible for many of the atrocities that have happened" because he headed the military at the time. "The horrific violence and persecution inflicted on the Rohingya cannot go unanswered," Miliband said.

The Foreign Office said it intends to bring in legislation targeting the export and supply of aviation fuel to Myanmar. It also committed an additional £5m to services for about 350,000 people in Rakhine state, and a further £3 million for accountability and justice for survivors of abuses across Myanmar.

The foreign ministers of Australia, Belgium, Canada, Cyprus, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Iceland, Latvia, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Portugal, Spain, The Gambia and the UK issued a joint statement. They said Myanmar had "violated its obligations under the Genocide Convention" and that the court's judgment is binding.

Miliband called on Myanmar to stop ongoing violations and to investigate, prosecute and punish perpetrators. He also urged an immediate pause in hostilities, an end to air strikes on civilians and the release of political prisoners.

He told MPs on Monday that the UK would raise the issue at the UN Security Council this week, with a dedicated meeting in a fortnight. MPs heard that air strikes and violence involving the Arakan Army are continuing.

The ICJ ruled on November 19, by nine votes to six among its judges, that "genocidal intent is the only reasonable inference that can be drawn from the evidence". It found that about 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2017 operation in Rakhine. Myanmar's government called the ruling unfair and a "great disappointment".
Britain expelled Myanmar's defence attaché after the verdict. Miliband said more than 1.2 million refugees fled and are being supported by Bangladesh.

stories.background: The ICJ ruling was the first time in the court's 80-year history that it found a state committed genocide, NDTV reported. Aung San Suu Kyi led Myanmar during the 2017 campaign and was deposed by the military in 2021.
stories.whyItMatters: The sanctions and planned fuel legislation add financial and supply restrictions on Myanmar's military leadership, while the aid funding targets about 350,000 people in Rakhine state.

stories.headline: SP and Congress agree broadly on UP seat-sharing, final numbers due in days
stories.dek: Both parties called the first round of talks in Delhi positive and will meet again on Tuesday, while Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya said the alliance would lose.
stories.summary: The Samajwadi Party and Congress said after a first round of talks in Delhi on Monday that they had a broad consensus on 2027 Uttar Pradesh seat-sharing, with a deal expected in two to three days. Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya said the alliance would 'lose badly'.
body: The Samajwadi Party (SP) and the Congress said on Monday they had reached a broad consensus on seat-sharing for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections after a first round of talks in Delhi, and expect to finalise the arrangement within two to three days.
The talks lasted about 15 minutes, according to The Times of India and The New Indian Express. Neither party disclosed how many seats are under discussion. The two sides are to meet again on Tuesday.

Ram Gopal Yadav, who led the SP delegation, said the meeting was cordial. "We will soon finalise this alliance and inform you. We expect to complete the process within the next two to three days," he told reporters.

UP Congress chief Aradhana Mishra, who led her party's team, called the discussions "positive" and "satisfactory". Asked about seat numbers, she said: "I cannot talk about numbers at the moment, but there is consensus."

Each side deputed four members. The Congress team included Mishra, UP in-charge Rajendra Pal Gautam, working president Imran Masood and MLA Virendra Chaudhary. The SP team included UP unit chief Shyam Lal Pal and MPs Rajeev Rai and Iqra Hasan.

The Congress had earlier sought 175-200 seats in the 403-member Assembly. SP chief Akhilesh Yadav had said publicly that the Congress was asking for 181 seats, which Congress sources said caused some unease in their camp. PTI reported that the Congress gave the SP its list of preferred constituencies on Monday.

Congress sources told The Times of India the party has identified around 140-150 constituencies for negotiation and hopes for more than 100 seats. They said about 60 high-priority seats are in Category A, with others in Categories B and C.

The SP has stressed winnability over a fixed formula. Akhilesh Yadav said: "Winnability is the only formula which can defeat the BJP in 2027." Tuesday's talks are expected to focus on constituency-wise organisational strength and caste equations.

Separately, Uttar Pradesh Deputy Chief Minister Keshav Prasad Maurya dismissed the alliance. "The SP-Congress alliance is no problem for us. The SP-Congress alliance is going to lose badly. The BJP is going to win with a full majority," he told reporters, according to ANI.
Maurya said the BJP's election preparations were "very solid, very comprehensive" and that the party aimed for a third consecutive term in the state.
The two parties contested the 2024 Lok Sabha elections together in the INDIA bloc. In Uttar Pradesh, the SP won 37 seats and the Congress six.

stories.headline: FSSAI sanctions prosecution of Bisleri over unsafe water sample; company disputes findings
stories.dek: Bisleri says it has received no notice and that independent tests found bromate within limits, while the regulator widens sampling of major packaged water brands.
stories.summary: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a sample from its Goa plant was declared unsafe. Bisleri says its water is safe, disputes the lab findings and says it has received no notice.
body: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) said on Sunday it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International after a packaged drinking water sample from its premises was declared unsafe, a finding the company disputed on Monday.

The regulator said the sample was non-compliant with prescribed bromate limits and was declared unsafe under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. After the company appealed, the referral food laboratory also declared it unsafe, this time after detecting polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), the FSSAI said in a social media post.

In a statement, the FSSAI said the law makes the referral lab's report final when a food business operator appeals. It said a prohibition-on-sale order was issued for Batch No. Go 270, that only one batch was found non-compliant, and that Bisleri has been asked to carry out a root cause analysis.
Bisleri said its water is safe for consumption. It said the matter concerns a batch made in September 2025 at its Goa facility, one of 143 plants in its network, and dates back about 14 months.
According to the company, the FSSAI collected six samples on September 30, 2025. Five met standards. The sixth showed bromate at 12 micrograms per litre against a prescribed limit of 10.

Bisleri said it appealed on November 22, 2025. The referral laboratory found bromate within the limit but separately flagged PAHs, the company said. It then had the same sample tested at an FSSAI-approved laboratory, which also found bromate within the limit.

The company said it sent those results to the FSSAI's Western Regional Office in a letter dated February 2, 2026, and heard nothing further. "To date, Bisleri has received no notice by email or in hard copy and has been unable to locate the reported notice on FSSAI's website," it said. A spokesperson told The Hindu that management is deciding on next steps.
Bisleri said it runs more than 90 tests across a 10-step manufacturing process and will cooperate with the FSSAI through the appropriate regulatory process.

NDTV, citing sources, reported that the FSSAI has collected samples of major packaged water brands and inspected manufacturing facilities, and is expected to begin legal proceedings against companies that fail tests. The Indian Express reported that the FSSAI also sanctioned prosecution against Vasant Masala, Tit-Bit Foods India, Mimansa Industries and Asha Confectionery, and suspended the licences of Urmi Lifesciences LLP and Gaur Ayurvedic Store.
keyFacts: FSSAI announced on Sunday, November 22, that it had sanctioned prosecution against Bisleri International.
The sample came from a Goa plant; the FSSAI says it was Batch No. Go 270.
Bisleri says the sixth of six samples showed bromate at 12 µg/l against a limit of 10.
Bisleri says it has received no notice and its water is safe.
The FSSAI is reportedly sampling other major packaged water brands, according to NDTV's sources.
stories.background: Bromate can form when ozone used to disinfect water reacts with bromide ions. The WHO has a provisional guideline value of 10 micrograms per litre for it, and the International Agency for Research on Cancer classes it as possibly carcinogenic to humans. PAHs are a group of organic compounds, some of which are carcinogenic. The Indian Express reported that 333 of 1,300 packaged water samples tested in 2023-24 were found non-conforming.
stories.whyItMatters: Sanctioned prosecution is not a judicial finding of guilt, but it moves the dispute towards legal proceedings. Other packaged water brands may face testing and possible action.

stories.headline: Bangladesh says it will arrest Hasina if she returns from India
stories.dek: Garment workers have rejected a pay offer of about 15%, adding to unrest as Awami League supporters hold protests over her planned December return.
stories.summary: State Minister Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters that Sheikh Hasina would be jailed if she returned to Bangladesh, and that Dhaka wants India to extradite her. Separately, garment workers rejected a wage offer of about 15%, with factories shut near Dhaka.
body: Bangladesh will arrest and jail former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina if she returns from India, State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam told Reuters in an interview on Sunday.

"As soon as she tries to enter Bangladesh, she will be arrested. And she will be taken to jail, and the law will take its course," Obaed said. Dhaka wants India to honour an existing extradition treaty and return Hasina "as a convict", she said.

India's foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In April, it said it was examining Bangladesh's extradition request. Obaed said there had been no official discussions with India about sending an aircraft to bring Hasina back.

Hasina has lived in India since fleeing Dhaka in August 2024 as protests demanded her resignation. She faces a death sentence in Bangladesh, and her Awami League party is banned. The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the 2024 unrest.

Hasina has planned to return in December and has sought a new passport and identity card, which the government has rejected. The Awami League this month announced a week of protests and rallies backing her return, ending in a nationwide lockdown on November 19.

Local media reported that police have recorded dozens of crude bomb blasts and arson attacks on vehicles in at least 28 districts over 10 days, injuring several police officers and civilians. Obaed called the violence a survival tactic by Hasina's "politically bankrupt political party". Khalid Mahmud Chowdhury, a senior Awami League official, said the current political establishment was responsible for the violence.
Obaed said Dhaka wanted balanced ties with New Delhi that did not compromise Bangladesh's "dignity, self-respect and interests".

Garment workers have also been protesting. Al Jazeera reported that they rejected a pay offer on Monday. Industry leaders had told Reuters, speaking anonymously, that manufacturers could propose a rise of roughly 15% in the minimum monthly wage, currently 12,500 taka ($100).
Workers want 30,000 taka ($242), citing food, housing and transport costs. Industry leaders said an increase above 15% would be unsustainable given rising costs and weak global demand.

Unrest continued on Monday and forced dozens of factories to close in Ashulia and Gazipur, near Dhaka. Police have used tear gas and sound grenades on demonstrators, according to Reuters. A survey by the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association found 18 days of disruption caused losses of about $428 million in 317 factories.
keyFacts: Shama Obaed Islam said Hasina would be arrested and jailed on entering Bangladesh.
Hasina has lived in India since August 2024 and faces a death sentence in Bangladesh.

Disruption caused losses of about $428 million in 317 factories, a manufacturers' survey found.
stories.background: Hasina's long rule ended after the 2024 uprising, and her Awami League has since been banned. Bangladesh is the world's second-largest garment exporter, with over 4 million workers in the sector, which supplies retailers including H&M, Gap and Walmart and generates more than 80% of export earnings, according to Reuters.
stories.whyItMatters: The standoff over Hasina's return and the wage dispute both affect stability in Bangladesh and its ties with India. The garment unrest also threatens an industry that provides most of the country's export earnings.

stories.headline: BRO says excavators at Sheshnag Lake are widening existing Amarnath track
stories.dek: Kashmiri political leaders, a cleric and environmentalists demanded a halt after a video showed machinery at the glacial lake, one of 14 listed as high-risk in Jammu and Kashmir.
stories.summary: The Border Roads Organisation said on Monday that post-Yatra work at Sheshnag Lake follows environmental safeguards and is confined to existing tracks. Leaders including Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, Mohit Bhan and M Y Tarigami called for the work to stop.
body: The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) said on Monday that excavators seen near Sheshnag Lake on the Amarnath Yatra route are widening existing tracks after the pilgrimage, as political leaders, a religious leader and environmental activists demanded the work be stopped.

A video showing an excavator creating a road near the lake, in Anantnag district, circulated widely on social media. It was first posted on an Instagram account named 'Neeraj_excavator_lover', according to The Indian Express. The account holder has since deleted it. The paper reported that the footage also shows soil being dumped on the lake's shores.

In a statement, the BRO, which comes under the Ministry of Defence, said it was carrying out "post-Amarnathji yatra works in compliance with all the applicable safety norms and environmental safeguards". It said it ensures safe disposal of excavated material, protects natural drainage and minimises disturbance to surrounding terrain.

The BRO said the video's claim of new works was incorrect. It said it had started widening tracks and stabilising vulnerable stretches, based on past Yatra experience and a requirement for a wider road, "to ease congestion and allow safer passage". It said the works are confined to existing tracks and serve the larger public interest. The Indian Express noted that the BRO did not explain why earth movers were being used at such altitude.

Sheshnag is one of 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu and Kashmir, according to Hindustan Times and NDTV. The Indian Express put its altitude at 3,590 metres and said it is reached by a 23-kilometre trek from Chandanwari near Pahalgam.

Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, the chief cleric of Srinagar's Jamia Masjid, called the visuals "very disturbing" and said the work "must be immediately stopped". He said improving facilities for pilgrims had never been an issue, "but not at the cost of our fragile ecosystem".

Mohit Bhan of the Peoples Democratic Party called it a "crime against Hinduism and faith in nature". He said Sheshnag is where Lord Shiva is believed to have left his serpents before proceeding to the Amarnath cave.

CPI(M) leader M Y Tarigami said the lake is surrounded by loose moraine and steep slopes. He asked the government to publish details of the project, the agency carrying it out and the clearances obtained, and to send glaciologists and environmental experts to the site. Congress leader Pawan Khera said the lake is sacred to both Hindus and Muslims.

Former MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi said Kashmir's mountains are "not BJP's real estate". Apni Party chief Altaf Bukhari asked the authorities to clarify whether the video is genuine. Former chief minister Mehbooba Mufti said the issue was painful and that the party fears being accused of opposing the Yatra if it says more.
Climate activist Raja Muzaffar Bhat asked on X how such heavy machines reached the glaciers of Kashmir. Several leaders cited the recent glacier-related floods in Nepal.
No government response beyond the BRO statement had been reported by Monday evening.
keyFacts: Sheshnag Lake is one of 14 high-risk glacial lakes identified in Jammu and Kashmir.
The BRO said work is confined to existing tracks and follows environmental safeguards.
The video was first posted on Instagram and later deleted by the account holder.
Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, Mohit Bhan, M Y Tarigami and Pawan Khera demanded a halt or disclosure.
Sheshnag lies on a 23-kilometre trek from Chandanwari in Pahalgam.
stories.background: Sheshnag is an alpine lake fed by glaciers, about one kilometre long and 0.7 kilometre wide, on the trekking route from Pahalgam to the Amarnath cave shrine. It is covered by snow for much of the year. Hindu tradition holds that Lord Shiva left his serpents there on the way to the cave.
stories.whyItMatters: Tarigami said the risks extend to people downstream, including Pahalgam and areas along the Lidder and across south Kashmir. The dispute also bears on how the Amarnath route is upgraded for pilgrims.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike agrees to buy Zscaler in $43.9 billion all-stock deal
stories.dek: Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each share held, and the deal is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028.
stories.summary: CrowdStrike agreed on Monday to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal, its largest acquisition to date. CrowdStrike shares fell 9% while Zscaler rose nearly 18%.
body: CrowdStrike has agreed to buy Zscaler for $43.9 billion in an all-stock deal, the companies announced on Monday, combining two cybersecurity firms as businesses seek stronger defences against attacks that use artificial intelligence.

Under the terms, Zscaler shareholders will receive 1.135 CrowdStrike shares for each Zscaler share. The deal is subject to regulatory approval. CNBC reported it is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike's fiscal year 2028, and TechCrunch said around this time next year.
CrowdStrike shares dropped 9% on Monday, while Zscaler shares rose nearly 18%, according to CNBC.

Zscaler, based in San Jose, California, provides cloud security products to about 8,000 enterprise companies, TechCrunch reported. Its zero-trust technology requires employees to authenticate each time they access an internal system or resource. CrowdStrike, based in Austin, Texas, secures devices connected to company networks and said it will join its endpoint protection software with Zscaler's platform.

The companies said the combination would create the "largest single addressable market" for cybersecurity and help customers adopt AI safely. CrowdStrike chief executive George Kurtz said in a statement: "With Zscaler, we're building cybersecurity's operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely."

The deal is CrowdStrike's biggest acquisition and takes it into the network security market, CNBC reported. The two companies had a combined market value above $265 billion at Friday's close, behind Palo Alto Networks at $282 billion.
JPMorgan analysts wrote that adding Zscaler could bring more breadth "in an era of vendor consolidation" and position CrowdStrike for rising demand for what they called AI sovereignty.

CrowdStrike also reported better-than-expected fiscal third-quarter results on Monday: earnings of 34 cents per share on $1.58 billion in revenue, against LSEG forecasts of 31 cents on $1.53 billion. Zscaler's fiscal first-quarter earnings, released the same day, also beat estimates.
keyFacts: Deal value is $43.9 billion, paid entirely in CrowdStrike stock.
Zscaler holders get 1.135 CrowdStrike shares per Zscaler share.

Combined market value exceeded $265 billion at Friday's close.
Closing is subject to regulatory approval.
stories.background: CNBC reported that cybersecurity deal-making has been heavy this year. Google announced plans last year to acquire Wiz for $32 billion, and Cisco paid about $28 billion for Splunk in 2024. Palo Alto Networks closed a $25 billion deal for CyberArk earlier this year.
stories.whyItMatters: The deal would merge two large security vendors serving enterprise customers, and analysts cited by CNBC say it could narrow CrowdStrike's gap with market leader Palo Alto Networks.

stories.headline: Anthropic mathematician posts apparent proof of Riemann hypothesis made with AI
stories.dek: Levent Alpöge says he built the 250,000-page proof over six weeks with Anthropic's Claude; a Lean-linked group backs it, while another mathematicians' body disputes that certainty is possible.
stories.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted on November 20 what he says is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, developed with the Claude AI tool. Two groups working on the Lean software have expressed full confidence in it, but mathematicians are still working to understand it.
body: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, posted on November 20 an apparent proof of the Riemann hypothesis, a problem dating to 1859, saying he developed it over six weeks with the company's AI tool Claude, Science News reported.
In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he worked alongside Claude. He also claims to have proved the generalised Riemann hypothesis, a broader form that extends the idea to related functions.

The next day, a joint statement from the Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative said independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," it read.

The proof runs to 250,000 pages. Claude, which can use outside tools as an AI agent, checked its work with Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code to test whether a chain of logic holds. It also drew on Mathlib, a library of known arguments already written in Lean. The exact version of Claude used has not been disclosed.

Mathematicians worldwide are still working to translate the proof into a form people can follow. Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia said it draws on many areas of mathematics. "I don't know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind," he said.

Not everyone accepts the framing. The Association for Human Mathematics said in a November 20 statement on its website that no human can claim responsibility for the proof, and that no mathematician can "confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct."

Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist at New York University, questioned how far the result extends. AI's strength at mathematics may not carry over to open-ended problems in biology, business or robotics, he wrote in a Substack post. "It's not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for," he wrote.

Bryna Kra of Northwestern University said the work was not produced by AI alone. Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of mathematicians, she said, and Alpöge is an experienced mathematician who did not simply request a proof and wait. She has criticised cases where AI agents worked largely without human input, such as OpenAI's recent solution to a puzzle on the Navier-Stokes equations. "There is someone to stand behind [the work]," she said.
Kra said she hoped the result would not be seen as an end to mathematics. "I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers," she said.
keyFacts: Levent Alpöge of Anthropic posted the proof on November 20.
He says he worked with Claude for six weeks.
The proof runs to 250,000 pages and was checked using Lean software.
Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative said they have full confidence in it.
The Association for Human Mathematics says full certainty cannot be confirmed.
stories.background: The Riemann hypothesis, dating to 1859, concerns the zeros of the Riemann zeta function, which are closely related to prime numbers. It says that certain zeros, of which there are infinitely many, all lie on one line on a graph. If true, it would show how many primes exist below a given number.
stories.whyItMatters: Much of mathematics involves prime numbers, so many other statements depend on the hypothesis being correct. Ono described the proof as "an earthquake throughout mathematics".

stories.headline: Mexican soldiers fired on after arrest of FBI most-wanted cartel leader
stories.dek: Mexico says no US agents took part in the operation that captured Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, though Washington supplied intelligence.
stories.summary: Mexico's defence ministry said eight suspected cartel members were detained after firing on soldiers in Sinaloa on Sunday, following the arrest of Fausto Isidro Meza Flores. President Claudia Sheinbaum said US agents did not take part in the operation.
body: Mexican soldiers on patrol in the town of Sinaloa de Leyva came under fire on Sunday, and the army detained eight alleged cartel members, Mexico's defence ministry said. The attack followed the arrest of cartel leader Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, known as "El Chapo Isidro", who was on the FBI's 10 most-wanted list.

The ministry said the soldiers were trying to restore order in northern Sinaloa state after violence that followed the arrest. It said the eight had also taken part in retaliatory attacks by Meza Flores's group in the hours after he was detained. One of the detainees was under age. Special forces also seized six vehicles, two of them armoured and fitted with gun turrets, the ministry said.
Sources differ on the day of the arrest. BBC News reported it as Friday, while Bloomberg, carried by Mint, said Saturday. The New York Times also gave Friday.

At her regular morning press conference on Monday, President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexican forces planned and led the operation, with no US agents on the ground. "The areas in which we coordinate with the US are security and intelligence. That was the agreement we reached from the start," she said. "But they do not conduct operations in Mexico." She confirmed that Mexican officials had asked the US to deploy a drone to help, without giving details.

Defence Minister Ricardo Trevilla said at the same press conference that security forces killed 16 alleged associates of Meza Flores and detained another 16 in the operation. Four soldiers were killed and ten federal agents were injured, he said. The operation involved hundreds of troops, special forces and several Black Hawk helicopters.

The US Department of Justice called the arrest "a spectacular military operation" and said the US Homeland Security Task Force had supported Mexican forces. US Ambassador Ronald Johnson pointed to intelligence sharing in a post on X. Washington has not claimed responsibility for the strike, according to Bloomberg.

US Assistant Attorney General A Tysen Duva called Meza Flores "the most dangerous man in Mexico". Meza Flores, 44, faces extradition to the US. Washington had offered a $5 million reward for information leading to his arrest or conviction.
keyFacts: Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, 44, was arrested in Sinaloa state and faces extradition to the US.

stories.background: Meza Flores heads the Guasave Cartel, named after a city in Sinaloa. The US Treasury identified him as a cartel leader in 2013 and said his group fought a turf war with the Sinaloa cartel. According to Bloomberg, the arrest is Mexico's highest-profile cartel operation since the February capture of Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera, who died of his injuries. Sheinbaum has faced pressure from US President Donald Trump to act more aggressively against cartels.
stories.whyItMatters: The case shows the limits Mexico's government sets on US involvement, as Sheinbaum says Washington shares intelligence but does not conduct operations in Mexico.

stories.headline: Supreme Court suspends life sentence of Godhra train-burning convict on medical grounds
stories.dek: The Gujarat government did not oppose the plea by Irfan Siraj Pada, who has spent about 18 years in jail and has serious cardiovascular disease.
stories.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentence of Irfan Siraj Pada, a convict in the 2002 Godhra train-burning case, citing serious heart disease. The order is not an acquittal, and his appeal against conviction remains pending.
body: The Supreme Court on Monday suspended the life sentence of Irfan Siraj Pada, a convict in the 2002 Godhra train-burning case, on medical grounds after he spent about 18 years in prison.
A bench of Justices MM Sundresh and PB Varale noted that Pada has serious cardiovascular disease. The Times of India reported that the state accepted his medical condition.

"Counsel for state submits that condition of the petitioner as submitted by the senior counsel appearing for the petitioner is factually correct. In view of the aforementioned factual scenario, we are inclined to grant suspension of sentence to the petitioner on medical grounds," the bench said.

Scroll, citing Bar and Bench, reported that the Gujarat government's counsel told the court the case involved a serious offence but that the state had no objection to suspension of the sentence given Pada's health.

The order does not amount to an acquittal. Pada's appeal against his conviction is pending before the Supreme Court, Scroll reported, citing Deccan Herald. Scroll also reported that the court has earlier granted bail to several other convicts in the case.

On February 27, 2002, coach S6 of the Sabarmati Express was set on fire at Godhra railway station. The Times of India put the death toll at 58, while Scroll reported 59 deaths. Scroll said the coach carried kar sevaks returning from Ayodhya.

In March 2011, a trial court convicted 31 people. Eleven were sentenced to death and 20 to life imprisonment, while 63 others were acquitted. In 2017, the Gujarat High Court commuted the 11 death sentences to life terms and upheld the other 20 life sentences.
The convicts' appeals have been pending in the Supreme Court since 2018, according to The Times of India.
